summary: Describes how Network Address Translator devices operate and defines terminology for the different kinds of NAT. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A NAT device lets many computers on a private network share one or more public addresses. RFC 2663 defines the terms for the different kinds of NAT and explains what each style allows and where applications can run into trouble.

questions: what is the difference between basic nat and napt
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the different kinds of Network Address Translator, and what each kind does and does not allow.

tldr.problem: The term Network Address Translator meant different things to different people, so it was hard to talk about what a NAT does, how it behaves and what applications it breaks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the core concepts (address realm, session, ALG) and names the main types of NAT: Basic NAT, NAPT, Bi-directional NAT, Twice NAT and Multihomed NAT, along with Realm Specific IP (RSIP).
tldr.outcome: It gives a consistent terminology and catalogs the common limits: applications that carry IP addresses in their payload need ALGs, and many end-to-end IPsec setups do not work across a NAT. The document is informational and has no updates or obsoletions listed.

today: RFC 2663 is an Informational document. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoletes or updates it, and it does not cover IPv6. It remains a standard terminology reference for IPv4 NAT behavior and its limitations.

sections.title: Why NAT Exists and What It Tries to Do
sections.content:
Network Address Translation maps IP addresses from one address realm to another to give hosts transparent routing. A NAT is typically placed at the border between a private network with unregistered addresses and an external network with globally unique, registered addresses. This document is limited to IPv4.

All NATs share three traits: transparent address assignment, transparent routing through address translation, and translation of ICMP error packet payloads. NAT modifies addresses in the IP header so datagrams can cross realms and keeps state for sessions so replies go to the right end node.

This approach only works when applications do not use IP addresses as part of the protocol itself. When they do, a NAT must be paired with an application level gateway (ALG), an application-specific translation agent. The RFC also notes that IPsec techniques which protect the IP header endpoints (such as AH and ESP) generally do not work across a NAT, because NAT alters the addresses those checks cover.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT is a border device that rewrites addresses so computers in a closed network can talk to the wider Internet using fewer public addresses. It can do this only if a message does not need its own address to be understood; otherwise, each such application must be handled specially.

sections.title: Sessions, Timeouts and Private Addresses
sections.content:
NAT translation is session based. A TCP or UDP session is identified by (source IP, source TU port, target IP, target TU port). An ICMP query session is identified by (source IP, ICMP query ID, target IP). Other sessions use (source IP, target IP, IP protocol). The first packet of the session determines its direction.

The start and end of sessions differ by protocol. A TCP session starts with a SYN and no ACK; it can be treated as ended four minutes after FINs are acknowledged or an RST is seen (the TIME-WAIT idea from RFC 793). For UDP and other protocols, there is no deterministic start or end, so heuristics are used and session timeouts must be configurable. Because a NAT cannot be sure packets will reach their destination, these timeouts are a practical trade-off.

Private networks commonly use the blocks set aside in RFC 1918: 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. Organizations using them must renumber or use NAT if they want to communicate with the public Internet or with other private networks that cannot share the same space.
sections.plainLanguage: To know where to send replies, the NAT keeps track of each conversation. A TCP conversation has clear start and end signals, but a simple UDP exchange has none. The NAT must make a best guess about when a conversation is finished and forget it. Many private networks use standard private address ranges so they do not clash with public addresses.

sections.title: How Address Translation Works
sections.content:
NAT performs three phases: address binding (associating a private address with an external address, either statically or dynamically at session start), address lookup and translation (rewriting IP addresses and, in some cases, transport identifiers for packets in the session), and address unbinding (freeing the binding when the last session using it ends). A single binding can be used for many simultaneous sessions from the same host.

The document also requires translation of certain ICMP error packets: Destination-Unreachable, Source-Quench, Time-Exceeded and Parameter-Problem. The Redirect message type must not be modified. When translating ICMP errors, the original IP packet embedded in the payload (and its transport header where present) must be updated, and the checksums (including the ICMP header checksum) must be adjusted so the packet remains correct after translation.
sections.plainLanguage: When a conversation starts, the NAT notes which inside computer is talking to which outside address and assigns a public address if needed. It then rewrites every packet in that conversation to carry the right addresses and forgets the mapping when the conversation ends. If an error message from the network refers back to that packet, the NAT must fix the quoted addresses inside the error so the original sender can understand it.

sections.title: Flavors of NAT
sections.content:
The RFC classifies several common types of NAT.

  • Basic NAT. Only the source (or destination, depending on direction) IP address is translated, using a block of external addresses. Sessions are outbound-only in the traditional model.
  • NAPT (Network Address Port Translation). Also translates transport identifiers (TCP/UDP ports or ICMP query IDs), so many private hosts can share a single external address. This is combined with Basic NAT in some cases.
  • Bi-directional NAT. Sessions can start from either side. It relies on a DNS-ALG to translate addresses in DNS queries and responses so external hosts can resolve and reach private hosts by name.
  • Twice NAT. Both source and destination addresses are translated. It is used when the private and external realms have address collisions. It also typically requires a DNS-ALG.
  • Multihomed NAT. Uses multiple NAT boxes or multiple links to provide fail-safe backup. For backup NATs to take over sessions transparently on failure, they must share or exchange state information; this is simpler when using static address bindings.

The RFC is careful to note: there is no 'Once-NAT'; translating both addresses is called Twice NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: Different NATs offer different trade-offs. Some only let computers inside call out. Others let people outside call in if names are handled correctly. A few must rewrite both the sender and the intended receiver when two networks accidentally use the same address range. To survive a broken connection, some setups keep spare helpers that need to know the same conversation state.

sections.title: Realm Specific IP (RSIP)
sections.content:
Realm Specific IP (RSIP) is a different approach: a host in the private realm assumes an address from the external realm so that packets between peers carry end-to-end addresses and need no translation along the path. An RSIP server sits in both realms to help route those packets inside the private network.

The document defines two variants. RSA-IP means the client adopts an external IP address. Packets can be tunneled within the private realm to the border or routed in other ways that allow the external addresses to be carried end to end. RSAP-IP means the client adopts an (external address, transport identifier) tuple, so several hosts share a single external address and communication is limited to TCP, UDP and ICMP sessions.

RSIP is presented as an alternative model; the RFC does not require it, but explains how it avoids some of the translation effects (particularly for address-carrying payloads) while introducing its own routing and security constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of rewriting letters as they pass through a receptionist, some computers borrow a proper outside address and send their letters inside a special envelope through the building. That way the addresses stay the same end to end, but the building still has to know how to deliver those envelopes.

sections.title: What Breaks and Security Notes
sections.content:
NATs touch only IP, TCP, UDP and ICMP headers and ICMP error messages. They do not modify application payloads. Two main trouble areas are payloads that contain IP addresses (or transport identifiers), and end-to-end security.

FTP is a classic example: the PORT command and the PASV response carry an address and port in ASCII. An FTP ALG must rewrite them, and changing the ASCII length can require adjusting TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers for the rest of the control connection.

IPsec: AH and ESP integrity checks cover the header fields that NAT rewrites (including addresses and the transport checksum), so packets fail the integrity check if addresses are changed. Transport-mode IPsec generally does not work through a NAT. IPsec tunnel mode ESP can work in cases where the tunnel endpoints handle the outer header appropriately (notably with RSIP-style arrangements or when the NAT is the tunnel endpoint). Application-layer security such as TLS, SSL and SSH works if it does not depend on IP addresses.

On the security side, traditional NAT can act as a rough one-way filter (blocking unsolicited sessions from outside) and dynamic address assignment makes targeted attacks harder. But ALGs, if placed outside a trusted boundary, could see user payloads. NAT devices themselves are Internet hosts and should be protected against SYN floods and ping floods like any server. The RFC also notes specific cautions for UDP multicast and partial matches on inbound UDP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: If an application writes an address inside its message (not just on the envelope), the NAT must open the message and fix that address too. If the message is sealed with a digital signature that covers the address, the seal breaks and the receiver will reject it. The NAT can help block unexpected callers, but it is not a full security wall by itself and must be defended like any other device on the network.
